To pine away means to slowly become weak, sad, and lifeless because of deep grief or intense longing for someone or something you have lost — or cannot have.

It is not just feeling sad. It is a consuming, wasting kind of sadness — the kind that eats away at you from the inside, day after day, until you lose your health, your energy, and your will to live.

Think of it like a slow fire that burns a person down to ash.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

"Pine" (the verb)

The word pine as a verb is very old. It comes from the Old English word pīnian, which meant to suffer or to cause suffering. And that Old English word itself came from the same ancient root as the word pain.

So from the very beginning, to pine meant to feel deep, aching pain — not a sharp physical pain, but a hollow, dull, emotional one. The kind of pain that sits in your chest and doesn't go away.

When you pine for someone or something, you feel a deep, intense longing. You desperately want that person or thing back, but you can't have them. That gap between what you want and what you have is the ache of pining.

"Away" (the particle)

Here, the word away does not mean a physical direction (like "walk away"). Instead, it works as an intensifier — it pushes the meaning further and adds a sense of gradual disappearance or continuous fading.

When you add "away" to a verb, you are often suggesting that something is happening slowly, continuously, and to the point of being used up:

  • Waste away → to gradually lose all strength and health
  • Fade away → to slowly disappear
  • Wither away → to slowly dry up and die
  • Pine away → to slowly lose yourself to grief

So "away" in this phrase tells you that the pining is not brief. It goes on and on, and it takes something from you little by little.
What It Looks and Feels Like

This phrase paints a very specific picture. When a person is pining away, they are not just crying in a corner for a day. Something much deeper and longer is happening:

  • They lose interest in food — they stop eating properly.
  • They lose interest in the things that once made them happy.
  • They become quieter, more withdrawn.
  • Their body starts to suffer — they lose weight, grow pale, become physically weak.
  • They seem absent, as if only their body is present but their mind is somewhere else.
  • They are slowly being hollowed out by their grief.

The phrase suggests that the longing or grief has become so powerful that it is literally destroying the person — their sadness is consuming their health and their life.

This is what makes "pine away" stronger and more serious than simply saying someone is sad or missing someone. Sadness is a feeling. Pining away is a condition — a state of being that takes over your entire existence.

In most uses, it is a person who pines away — typically because of:

  • The death of a deeply loved person (a spouse, a child, a close friend)
  • A failed or lost love (a lover who left or died)
  • Separation from one's homeland or family
  • A longing for something beautiful that is now gone forever

But the phrase is also used for animals, especially loyal pets. It is said, for example, that a dog can pine away after the death of its owner — refusing to eat, becoming listless, and slowly fading.

Here are some example sentences to show you how the phrase is actually used:

  • "After her son emigrated, she pined away for years, waiting for his letters."
    → She was consumed by grief and longing after losing daily contact with her son.
  • "The old man pined away after his wife passed — he barely ate, rarely spoke, and was gone within a year."
    → His grief was so deep that he slowly lost his health and his will to live.
  • "The dog refused to leave its owner's grave and pined away over the following weeks."
    → The dog was in such deep distress that it became physically weak.
  • "Don't pine away over someone who doesn't value you."
    → Don't waste yourself emotionally on a person who doesn't appreciate you.

Notice that in all these cases, the pining is long, slow, and deeply damaging.

"Pine away" is a phrasal verb — a verb combined with a particle (here, "away") that together create a specific meaning.

You use it in one of these patterns:

Pattern 1 — with no object (most common):
She pined away.
(No object follows. The person is simply consumed by grief.)

Pattern 2 — with "for" + the person or thing longed for:
He pined away for his lost love.
She pined away for her homeland.
(Here, "for" tells you what or who they are longing for.)

You would not say "she pined away her sadness" — that is grammatically wrong. The verb is used intransitively, meaning nothing directly receives the action.

This phrase carries a melancholic, literary, and somewhat old-fashioned tone.

You are more likely to find it in:

  • Classic literature and poetry
  • Historical novels or period dramas
  • Describing grief in a formal or poetic way
  • Songs and ballads of lost love

You are less likely to hear it in everyday casual conversation. If a friend misses their boyfriend, they would say "she really misses him" or "she's heartbroken" — not usually "she is pining away." But if the grief is deep and ongoing, a person might say it for extra emotional weight.

The phrase has a certain romantic tragedy to it — it brings to mind images of medieval knights waiting for their ladies, or Victorian widows slowly fading after losing their husbands. It evokes something grand and all-consuming, not ordinary sadness.
Related Phrases and How They Compare

Understanding related expressions helps you see exactly where "pine away" sits in the language:

"Pine for" (without "away"):
This simply means to long deeply for someone or something. It suggests the longing, but not necessarily the physical deterioration.
"I pine for the days of my childhood."
Milder than "pine away."

"Waste away":
To gradually lose all physical health and strength. It focuses more on the body deteriorating. Pine away includes emotional deterioration too.
"He wasted away in hospital."

"Languish":
To be in a state of weakness and neglect, often due to sadness or difficult circumstances. Similar to pine away but can apply to a wider range of situations, including being forgotten or stuck.
"She languished in an unhappy marriage."

"Yearn for":
To feel a strong, often wistful longing for something. Very similar to "pine for" but slightly more gentle. Does not carry the idea of physical deterioration.
"He yearned for his homeland."

"Grieve":
To feel grief, usually over a death. This is the broader emotion. Pine away is a specific way of grieving — slowly and to the point of wasting.
A Quick Summary to Carry With You

AspectDetail

To sum it up in plain words:

To pine away = to slowly fade and weaken, consumed by deep longing or grief for someone or something lost, to the point where your health and spirit both suffer.

It is sadness at its most absorbing — not a moment of pain, but a long, quiet surrender to loss.
One Last Image to Lock It In

Imagine a candle that is burning not because anyone lit it for a celebration, but because it was placed next to a grave. It flickers alone in the dark. No one comes. It doesn't go out quickly. It just slowly, quietly melts away — until nothing is left.

That is what it means to pine away.
